chunks: Optimizing pick-and-place paths. The question: Pick-and-place machines must often traverse repetitive paths for assembly. What are some optimizations?
A pick-and-place machine spends its time moving a head between a bank of part feeders and the board.
Optimizing it means setting up the job so the head wastes less time: a shorter route, parts on sensible feeders, fewer trips, and fewer tool swaps.
Even a small saving on each part adds up over thousands of boards.
Think of running errands. If you visit stores in a random order, you drive back and forth for nothing.
If you plan a sensible loop, and carry a basket so you can collect several items per trip, you finish much sooner. Putting the things you grab most often near the door helps too.
The machine's problems are the same: route, trips, and where things are stored.
The analogy breaks only on speed, since the machine's time depends on how fast it can accelerate, not just on distance.
Five levers, each a separate optimisation. Vendors solve them in stages; the order matters because feeder assignment changes pick distances and sequencing uses them.
Placement route: the order in which the head visits the board positions. Finding the shortest one is a classic puzzle called the traveling salesman problem.
Feeder assignment: which part reel sits in which slot of the feeder bank. Collect-and-place: a head with several nozzles that picks several parts, then places them.
Nozzle change: swapping the suction tip for a different size, which takes seconds. Bottleneck: the slowest machine in the line, which sets the pace for all of them.
A board has 400 parts. A head that carries one part per trip makes 400 trips. A head with 6 nozzles needs only 67 round trips, because 400 / 6 rounds up to 67.
Each trip carries more, so total travel time drops. Grouping parts by nozzle type also avoids swaps, and one swap can cost as much time as 5 to 10 placements.

I'd optimise the placement order, which is like a travelling-salesman problem, using heuristics like nearest-neighbour plus 2-opt; assign feeders so frequently used and co-placed parts are close to the board and to each other; use multi-nozzle collect-and-place to cut trips; group parts by nozzle to avoid changes; and balance parts across machines so no one is the bottleneck.
On the design side, fewer unique parts and common packages help too."
